newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian lawmakers scuttle extradition bill.
newsitem.headline: Colombian lawmakers scuttle extradition bill.

text.p: Lawmakers failed to approve the government's call for an end to Colombia's ban on extradition on Wednesday, opening the door to a new assault on the country's anti-drug efforts by Washington.

Interior Minister Horacio Serpa vowed that the government remained committed to seeing the ban lifted before President Ernesto Samper leaves office in August, 1998. "We didn't want to see what happened today," he said.

But Serpa, acting head of state until Samper returns from an official visit to the Mideast and Africa, conceded that the government faced an uphill battle in winning legislative approval of a practice that polls consistently show most Colombians oppose.
"You can't cover up the sun with your hands," Serpa said. "This is one of the most contentious issues there is."

After two days of heated debate, the constitutional affairs committee of the Senate voted 8-8 against approving a draft law that would lift the ban on extradition, which was imposed by Colombia's constituent assembly in 1991. A simple majority would have been sufficient to see the legislation was passed on to a plenary Senate session for further debate.

Since constitutional reforms must be approved by two consecutive sessions of Congress -- and the current session ends on June 20 -- lawmakers said Wednesday's vote virtually ruled out any chance of the ban being lifted this year.

Justice Minister Almabeatriz Rengifo told reporters that in cases involving a split decision the bill could be put to a second vote almost immediately. But several key lawmakers saw no chance for its passage.
"The bill has sunk," said Sen. Luis Guillermo Giraldo, a leading proponent of seeing Colombia's drug lords and other criminals tried in the United States and other countries.
"This is a defeat for the whole country," he added, saying the vote would add to Colombia's drug-tarnished image abroad and meant "becoming even more isolated from the international community."

The ban on extradition was approved by the constituent assembly after years of violence that saw hundreds of people, including three presidential candidates, a justice minister, high court judges, journalists and scores of police killed in a campaign of assassinations and bombings that drug lords waged against extradition in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Samper has been severely weakened by charges that he accepted millions of dollars in cocaine cash to finance his 1994 campaign.

His government failed to back earlier efforts to revive extradition, but he proposed a bill to restore the practice just eight days ago under intense pressure from Washington. The United States, which has "decertified" Colombia's counternarcotics efforts for the past two years, argues that detention in a secure U.S. prison facility is what Colombia's drug kingpins fear the most.
Not surprisingly, given Samper's own alleged ties to drug lords, the government took a beating from both sides of the Senate committee floor in the debate over its call to revive extradition.

Giraldo argued that the government secretly opposed its own legislation and had "got its way" by failing to lobby Senate committee members hard enough in its favour. "There won't be extradition before August 7," he said, referring to the date when Samper will hand over power next year.
Other lawmakers argued that extradition was tantamount to high treason, however, and accused the government of bowing and scraping in the face of demands from Washington.
